Aniline itself is strongly activating and o/p-directing, so on its own it would give almost no meta product.
But the nitrating mixture is strongly acidic, and the lone pair on –NH₂ is basic.
It is protonated: C₆H₅NH₂ + H⁺ ⇒ C₆H₅NH₃⁺, the anilinium ion.
That lone pair is now tied up, and the –NH₃⁺ group carries a full positive charge,
so it is strongly deactivating and meta-directing, like –NO₂.
The mixture therefore contains a sizeable share of m-nitroaniline.
∴ because in strong acid aniline exists as the anilinium ion.

kcet|Chemistry|2026|18||0|0.s:
In water the basicity of an alkylamine is a balance of three things.
(1) Inductive effect — alkyl groups push electron density onto N, making the lone pair more available.
(2) Solvation effect — the more N–H bonds the cation keeps, the better water can hydrogen bond to it and stabilise it.
(3) Steric hindrance — bulky alkyl groups block the proton's approach to the lone pair.
Together these are why the order in water is 2° > 1° > 3° rather than simply 3° > 2° > 1°.
(4) Hyperconjugation needs a π system or an empty/odd orbital next to the C–H bonds; an amine lone pair is neither.
∴ basic strength in aqueous phase is not decided by hyperconjugation.

Follow the chain one reagent at a time.
Benzene + conc. HNO₃/conc. H₂SO₄ at 323–333 K ⇒ A = nitrobenzene, C₆H₅NO₂.
A + Fe/HCl (reduction) ⇒ B = aniline, C₆H₅NH₂.
B + NaNO₂/HCl at 273 K (diazotisation) ⇒ C = benzene diazonium chloride, C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻.
C + C₂H₅OH loses N₂: ethanol acts as the reducing agent, handing a hydride to the ring.
Benzene is formed, and the ethanol is oxidised as it gives that hydrogen up.
C₂H₅OH ⇒ CH₃CHO, so the products are C₆H₆ + CH₃CHO + N₂ + HCl.
∴ D is CH₃CHO.

kcet|Chemistry|2026|20||0|0.s:
In staggered ethane the C–H bonds on the front carbon sit between those on the back carbon, 60° apart.
In eclipsed ethane they line up, so the bonding pairs are closest and repel most.
That repulsion between eclipsing bonds is the torsional strain.
So torsional strain is at a maximum in the eclipsed form and a minimum in the staggered form —
about 12.5 kJ mol⁻¹ separates them, with staggered the lower.
Statement I (staggered is more stable) is therefore true.
Statement II says the staggered form has more torsional strain, which is the reverse, so it is false.
∴ Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

kcet|Chemistry|2026|24||0|0:
Count the σ bonds and lone pairs on nitrogen in each, then read off the shape.
NO₂⁺ : 2 σ bonds, no lone pair on N ⇒ 2 electron domains ⇒ linear, 180° ⇒ sp.
NO₃⁻ : 3 σ bonds, no lone pair on N ⇒ 3 domains ⇒ trigonal planar, 120° ⇒ sp².
NH₄⁺ : 4 σ bonds, no lone pair ⇒ 4 domains ⇒ tetrahedral, 109°28′ ⇒ sp³.
Note all three are ions in which nitrogen keeps no lone pair, so the σ count alone decides it.
∴ sp, sp² and sp³ respectively.

Test each order against the real values.
(b) Bond angle: HgCl₂ is linear 180°, NH₄⁺ tetrahedral 109°28′, SF₆ octahedral 90° ⇒ the order holds.
(c) H-bond strength rises with the electronegativity of the atom carrying H: N < O < F ⇒ the order holds.
(d) Bond length follows atomic size, I > Br > Cl ⇒ H–I > H–Br > H–Cl holds.
(a) Dipole moment: BF₃ is trigonal planar and symmetric, so its bond dipoles cancel exactly, μ = 0.
In NF₃ the lone-pair moment opposes the three N–F moments, leaving only μ ≈ 0.23 D.
In NH₃ the lone pair and the N–H moments point the same way, giving μ ≈ 1.47 D.
The true order is NH₃ > NF₃ > BF₃, the reverse of the one printed.
∴ only (a) fails to agree.
kcet|Chemistry|2026|26||0|0:
Take the statements one by one.
(a) True — resonance makes all three C–O bonds identical, each of bond order 1⅓, all 1.29 Å.
(b) True — the double bond can be placed on any one of the three oxygens, giving three equivalent structures.
(c) False — in resonance only electrons are redistributed. The nuclei stay exactly where they are;
if atoms moved, the structures would be different compounds, not resonance forms.
(d) False — carbon has 4 bonds and no lone pair, so its formal charge is 0.
The 2– belongs to the oxygens, each carrying −⅔ on average.
∴ only (a) and (b) are correct.
kcet|Chemistry|2026|27||0|0:
Check each statement against the oxidation numbers.
Statement I: in H₂O₂ the O–O peroxide link gives each oxygen −1 ✓.
RbO₂ is a superoxide containing O₂⁻, so the charge is shared by two oxygens, −½ each ✓.
Statement I is correct.
Statement II: in HAuCl₄, H is +1 and each Cl is −1, so Au = +3, and HAu(III)Cl₄ is right.
In MnO₂ each O is −2, so Mn = +4, and the stock notation must be Mn(IV)O₂, not Mn(II)O₂.
Statement II is therefore incorrect.
∴ Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
